Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do

A flare-up is a sudden increase in disease activity — more pain, more swelling, more stiffness, more fatigue. They can last hours, days, or weeks, and they can strike even when you've been managing your condition well.

Recognising a Flare-Up

Common signs include:

  • Increased joint pain that doesn't respond to your usual measures
  • Morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes (or significantly longer than your baseline)
  • Swelling, warmth, or redness in one or more joints
  • Fatigue that feels disproportionate to your activity level
  • Difficulty with tasks you normally manage

Immediate Steps (First 24–48 Hours)

1. Rest — but don't stop completely Protect the affected joints, but gentle movement prevents stiffness from worsening. Think "modify, don't stop."

2. Apply cold for swelling, heat for stiffness

  • Ice packs (wrapped in a cloth) for 15 minutes to reduce acute swelling
  • Heat pads or warm baths for stiffness and muscle tension
  • Alternate if you have both symptoms

3. Review your medication If you have a "flare plan" from your rheumatologist, follow it. This might include a short course of anti-inflammatory medication or a temporary increase in pain relief. Never exceed recommended doses without medical advice.

4. Prioritise sleep Flare-ups worsen with poor sleep. Use pillows to support painful joints, keep the room cool, and consider a warm bath before bed.

Days 3–7: Active Recovery

  • Gentle stretching: 5–10 minutes twice daily to maintain range of motion
  • Anti-inflammatory nutrition: Increase omega-3 rich foods (salmon, mackerel, walnuts), reduce sugar and processed foods
  • Hydration: Dehydration increases joint pain sensitivity
  • Pacing: Use the 50% rule — do half of what you think you can manage

When to Contact Your GP or Rheumatologist

  • Flare lasts more than 7–10 days without improvement
  • You develop a fever alongside joint symptoms (could indicate infection)
  • A single joint becomes very hot, red, and swollen (rule out septic arthritis)
  • You're unable to perform basic daily tasks
  • Your mental health is significantly affected

Preventing Future Flare-Ups

  • Identify triggers: Common ones include stress, overexertion, weather changes, poor sleep, and illness
  • Keep a symptom diary: Note activities, food, stress levels, and weather alongside symptoms
  • Maintain medication consistency: Skipping doses is one of the most common flare triggers
  • Build rest into your routine: Don't wait until you're exhausted

Key Takeaway

Flare-ups are not a sign of failure. They're a normal part of living with arthritis. Having a clear plan means you can respond quickly and recover faster.

Practical next steps for Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do When Symptoms Get Worse

If you came here about Arthritis Flare-Up: What to Do When Symptoms Get Worse, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Talking with your clinician

Bring the bottle or a photo to pharmacy or clinic appointments. Pharmacists can flag interactions with methotrexate, anticoagulants and other common arthritis medicines. Document start dates so you and your team can judge benefit honestly after several weeks.

Quick questions about Arthritis Flare What When

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
